Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images This Is Europe World news Germany’s firewall was meant to hold the far right at bay. It may have done the reverse An AfD win in ​next month’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt would shatter a decades-long political consensus and reverberate throughout the EU Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Jon Henley Wed 19 Aug 2026 10.30 EDT Last modified on Wed 19 Aug 2026 11.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n just over two weeks’ time, Saxony-Anhalt – home to historic timber-framed houses, the dramatic Harz mountains and the birthplace of Martin Luther – will hold what could prove one of the most significant state elections in Germany’s postwar history. The vote, on 6 September, could see a far-right party whose local branch is officially classified by the country’s domestic intelligence service as “confirmed rightwing extremist” appoint a state premier and govern a state alone, for the first time. That could have big consequences for both Germany and Europe . With more state elections a fortnight later in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, it could also end the consensus that, since the second world war, has kept the far right at bay in Germany. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) has led most German national polls since April last year. It is comfortably ahead in eastern Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and is even second in famously liberal Berlin. In Saxony-Anhalt, the party – which dabbles in Nazi imagery, differentiates between “biological” and “passport” Germans, and whose rhetoric and policies are often way more extreme than many other EU far-right parties – is polling at up to 42%. Under Germany’s proportional representation threshold, which excludes parties that capture less than 5% of the vote, a score in the low-to-mid 40s could quite conceivably secure AfD an absolute majority in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. As the Centre for Strategic and International Studies points out , that would have an immediate domestic impact. Germany’s 16 states exercise constitutional authority over education, policing, public broadcasting and regional civil administration. AfD’s proposed state-level measures include revising the school history curriculum to emphasise Germany’s “achievements” over its wartime crimes, defunding anti-racism initiatives, removing pride flags and rewriting the mandates of public TV and radio. An AfD government could exploit state-level public recruitment criteria and make political appointments favouring ideologically aligned candidates, and, more broadly, create an intimidating environment where state employees prefer silence to conflict. At the federal level, winning a state government would also give the AfD seats in the Bundesrat upper house representing the states. That would not allow it to block legislation unilaterally, but it could table new policy initiatives and disrupt consensus. On the EU stage, while the party is somewhat sidelined within parliament – it heads the uber-nationalist ESN group, including France’s Reconquest and Italy’s National Future – its increased influence in Germany would weaken European unity. An increasingly fragmented German political landscape would undermine Berlin’s role as an engine of European integration, affecting decision-making in key areas such as environment policy (AfD rejects the need for climate action ). In other vital areas – such as policy towards Ukraine – a more influential AfD’s hostility to further military aid for Kyiv and eagerness to normalise relations with Moscow would directly benefit Russia’s efforts to sap western unity. More broadly, an AfD victory would be a potent signal that even the EU’s biggest economy is vulnerable to the far right, boosting nativist parties in countries with crunch national elections in the next 18 months, such as France, Italy, Spain and Poland. But there’s another dimension to a possible AfD victory in Saxony-Anhalt that deserves a closer look. For decades, Germany’s political parties have operated a so-called “Brandmauer”, or firewall, to prevent the normalisation of far-right extremism. A Brandmauer backfire View image in fullscreen Regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt will be a test for the ruling CDU party. Photograph: Filip Singer/EPA In essence, the firewall should rule out any form of coalition or structural cooperation with the AfD. In 2018, the centre-right CDU of Chancellor Friedrich Merz even codified the Brandmauer into a formal “incompatibility resolution”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The objective, of course, was to prevent support for the AfD increasing, its influence expanding, and, ultimately, the far-right party winning power. It hasn’t worked – and analysts now suggest there may be three distinct flaws with the firewall strategy. First, as The Economist argued , by making the AfD a political pariah, the Brandmauer has in effect insulated the party from the compromises and failures of government. With no need to deliver actual results, it can promise voters whatever it likes (and it does). That, of course, has made it even more appealing. Unlike many other European far-right parties that have experienced the accountability that accompanies regional or national power, the AfD has not been obliged to moderate its language or its ideas. Second, as the German academic Alexander Görlach observed , the firewall has “hollowed-out” the centre: to build majorities excluding the far right, the CDU has had to enter “Grand Coalitions” with its historic adversary, the centre-left SPD. Over time, this constant reliance on uncomfortable alliances and ideological compromise has blurred the distinctions between the mainstream parties, reinforcing the AfD’s line that the establishment forces are carbon-copy “cartel parties”. With the far-right party dominating polling in eastern Germany, the CDU’s rigid observance of the firewall has led it into unnatural, unstable and thus largely ineffective alliances, further frustrating voters and driving support for extremes. In 2018, four years before he became CDU leader, Merz promised to halve the AfD’s score. Since then, it has almost doubled. As elsewhere in Europe, shifting rightward, notably on immigration, has served only to validate the far right’s agenda . It could be, of course, that the AfD does not win an absolute majority on 6 September. But even if it does not, the CDU may be forced to ally with pretty much every other party in parliament, including the radical-left Die Linke, to keep it out. That, analysts suggest, may prove a bridge too far for some senior party figures, and could have dire, even fatal consequences for Merz’s leadership – at around 13%, his approval ratings are already among the lowest of any postwar chancellor. But the fate of Germany’s Brandmauer is worth pondering. That’s not to say it isn’t a good idea to try to isolate the far right. But if you don’t have the policies to actually beat it at the ballot box, the net result may be that the cycle of ideological compromises you are forced into merely alienates voters further – and drives them into the arms of the very far right you sought to contain. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yj.text: Image source, Getty Images By Kelly Ng Published 4 hours ago Thai police have arrested a Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling 100 million baht ($3m; Â£2.2m) from his monastery, along with a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with. Phra Wachirayan Wi, a former abbot at the prominent 14th-Century Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, allegedly pocketed donations meant for the temple on more than 20 occasions over two years. In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions. He was defrocked after his arrest. He has yet to comment publicly. The latest arrests come just over a year after another sex-and-blackmail case involving senior monks rocked Thailand's monastic community. The 66-year-old was known for creating a highly-coveted coin amulet. Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul reportedly owns some of his creations. Thailand's Buddhist institution has long been plagued with reports of monks breaking their vow of celibacy, trafficking drugs and committing financial crimes. In July last year, police opened a hotline for people to report "misbehaving monks" after at least nine monks were found to have had sex with a woman . She then blackmailed them with photos and videos of the acts for nearly $12 million. Police on Friday said they identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts Phra Wachirayan had issued in the temple's name â one was meant for temple renovations, while the other was payment for amulets and other sacred objects. "But the money from both streams did not enter the temple's account. Not a single baht," lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan told a news conference, according to reports. Police found cash and gold bars worth more than 100 million baht while raiding Phra Wachirayan's residence on Thursday, with counting going on until late into the night, Thai news outlet The Nation reported. While examining CCTV footage in the residence, police found a clip of him having sex with a woman on his dining table. Authorities identified her as 47-year-old Punyavee Rungrueang, who has been arrested on charges of abetting a state official in illegal activities. She has yet to comment publicly. Many monks in Thailand receive stipends from the government and are therefore considered state officials. Police seized 35 gold amulets, along with about 1.5kg of gold bars and jewellery, worth an estimated 6.04 million baht, from Punyavee's home. Police believe Punyavee helped Phra Wachirayan manage his embezzled proceeds, noting that tens of millions of baht circulated through her bank accounts each year, The Bangkok Post reported. Investigators say they started looking into the case in mid July, after receiving an anonymous tip alleging Phra Wachirayan of misconduct and misuse of temple funds. Two or three other people could be involved in the case, they say. https://www.mfa.gov.lv/en/article/baiba-.text: Baiba Braže: Closer EU–US economic and technological cooperation strengthens transatlantic security Published: 11.09.2026. Flickr Photo: Laura Celmiņa, Ministry of Foreign Affairs Facebook X / Twitter Linkedin Threads On 11 September 2026, in Riga, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, met with Andrew Puzder, the US Ambassador to the European Union. The talks focused on closer transatlantic economic cooperation as a means of strengthening security, competitiveness and resilience. Baiba Braže and Andrew Puzder discussed developments in EU–US trade and investment, as well as European competitiveness and economic security. The Minister emphasised Latvia’s interest in attracting US investment, promoting cooperation between businesses in the two countries, and diversifying supply chains through collaboration with reliable partners. Particular attention was paid to practical cooperation in the energy sector, the defence industry and new technologies, including artificial intelligence, quantum technologies and unmanned systems. Baiba Braže noted that a strong European economy and close EU–US economic relations also strengthen transatlantic security. The Minister of Foreign Affairs expressed her gratitude to the United States for its unwavering support for Latvia and its significant contribution to the security of Latvia and the Baltic region. To mark the 250th anniversary of US independence, a commemorative stamp issued in collaboration with Latvijas Pasts was unveiled at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The stamp symbolises the close ties between Latvia and the US, as well as the importance of freedom and transatlantic unity. During his visit, Andrew Puzder participated in a panel discussion at the Rīga Conference entitled “Two Years from The Draghi Report: The State of EU’s Competitiveness”, alongside Valdis Dombrovskis, European Commissioner for Economy and Productivity, and other experts. The discussion was focused on investment, regulatory simplification, technological capacity and transatlantic economic cooperation. The Ambassador’s agenda also included a meeting with representatives of the American Chamber of Commerce in Latvia, a visit to the IT cluster at Riga Technical University and a discussion with executives from technology companies, and meetings with Latvian officials. At the conclusion of the visit, a memorial event for the victims of the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks was held at the US Embassy. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw20.text: Image source, Tennessee Department of Corrections Image caption, If the execution proceeds, Christa Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years By Stephanie Hegarty ,Â World Service correspondent Â and Â Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 30 September 2026, 15:33 BST Updated 6 hours ago The execution of Tennessee inmate Christa Pike has been halted just over an hour before it was due to happen. Pike, 50, has been awaiting execution since she was convicted and sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer. In their ruling on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court said they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case. It is unclear how long the pause will last. This latest ruling comes after the Supreme Court denied a reprieve and the Tennessee governor declined to grant Pike's request for clemency earlier this week. Her lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee argued in court that Pike had lied about being sexually abused as a child. But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the State said it does not dispute she suffered sexual abuse and rape. Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected. The appeal that led to Wednesday's stay is different from that made to the Supreme Court, which refused to hear Pike's appeal. It came from her challenge to Tennessee's lethal injection method, which Pike's lawyers said could cause suffering beyond what is needed to carry out the death sentence - something the Constitution does not allow. The lawyers argued that Tennessee's procedures had denied Pike a fair chance to prove this. "We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue," Tennessee's Attorney General said in a statement. "It is common in capital cases for the defence to raise last minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the Supreme Court of the United States to lift the stay." Image source, Family handout Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was 19 when she was murdered in 1995 She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens. The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the teen was found with a pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the pentagram herself. She had accused Slemmer of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after and showed them a piece of Slemmer's skull. A year later, Pike was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence. Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. At the time of her incarceration, Pike was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections. https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/na.text: A man accused of murdering his 19-year-old stepdaughter was seen walking to her halls of residence with a blanket over his head the day before she was found dead, prosecutors allege. Nathan Owens, 34, denies murder, strangulation and grievous bodily harm charges relating to Carla Georgescu. Carla, a second-year psychology student at the University of Lancashire, was found dead at her student accommodation in Victoria Street, Preston, on February 5 - her 20th birthday. The jury at Preston Crown Court heard how Carla and her mother, Janina, spent the weekend of January 31 and February 1 shopping for presents and watching TV together, Lancashire Live reports. Janina said her daughter was "happy and excited" and looking forward to a trip to Romania on February 5. On February 1, Owens drove from the family home in Hartlepool to join Janina and Carla for a meal at Kimji Korean restaurant. At the end of the meal, Janina left her husband and daughter together at the table, the trial heard. The jury was shown footage of Owens arriving at Ribble Hall on February 1 and parking in the designated bays on campus. After the meal, Janina and Owens dropped Carla off at her accommodation before returning together to the east coast, the court heard. However, a second CCTV compilation showed Owens returning to Preston in the early hours of February 4. This time, he parked some distance from the university accommodation and covered his head with a blanket before making his way to the student block, prosecutor Nicholas Lumley KC told the jury. Mr Lumley said: "Why choose to go that night? We may never know. He would have known that Carla was due to leave for Romania the next day, to go with her friend on a trip to that country. "He would have known she had struck up a romantic relationship with a young man who she also planned to see in the near future. It could have been there was a degree of sexual jealousy. Did he not want her to be romantically involved with anyone else?" The prosecution alleges Owens stabbed and strangled Carla before leaving her in her bedroom. She was found slumped against her wardrobe on February 5, with injuries to her head and defensive marks on her hands, as well as sexual injuries. A belt was tightly wrapped around her neck, the jury was told. Carla's mother asked campus security to check on her daughter after she failed to answer calls or messages on her birthday. When officers discovered her body, they initially thought she had taken her own life, the court heard. However, the prosecution alleges that in the week before Carla’s death, Owens viewed videos of himself having sex with an effigy dressed in her nightdress and with her toy dolls. Mr Lumley said: "Her death was the culmination, the end point, of weeks, months and perhaps years of a one-sided sexual obsession. "And it was the beginning of a complex murder investigation, which led to his door in Hartlepool. It was he who was sexually fixated on Carla, and it was he, Nathan Owens, who had killed Carla." The trial continues.
